premise: A period drama set at MIT in 1966, the year Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA.
title: ELIZA · 1966
overview: MIT in 1966 was an institution reshaped by federal defense grants and computing experiments. Joseph Weizenbaum built the ELIZA script inside Project MAC at 545 Technology Square. Staff members, researchers, and students interacted with the software across shared teletype terminals. The film follows a university bystander observing human self-delusion with comedic irony.

boxes.name: COMPUTING HARDWARE INTERACTION
boxes.description: Gather technical manuals, photographs, and user accounts detailing the physical operation of the IBM 7094 and compatible teletype terminals in MIT Project MAC offices during 1966.
boxes.rationale: Actors and technical crew require exact operational knowledge of keypunch machines, terminal interfaces, and paper-tape handling to stage ELIZA interaction scenes convincingly.
boxes.summary: Project MAC operated large IBM 7094 mainframe computers connected to remote teletype terminals. Technical manuals define the machine through its physical console, magnetic tapes, and time-sharing protocols. Operators typed text inputs directly into terminal units to receive printed responses. These paper printouts served as the physical surface for user interaction with programs like ELIZA.

boxes.name: PROJECT MAC INTERIORS
boxes.description: Examine floor plans, interior photographs, and lighting schemes of the Technology Square complex at MIT where the Project MAC artificial intelligence laboratories were housed.
boxes.rationale: The production designer must replicate the specific fluorescent lighting, modular office partitions, and machine-room layout that framed Weizenbaum's daily work environment.
boxes.summary: The Project MAC artificial intelligence laboratories occupied facilities at 545 Technology Square. Floor plans and photographic records show modular office interiors with fluorescent overhead lighting. Administrative records designate the site as a hub for Robert Fano and J.C.R. Licklider's computing initiatives. The modern architecture housed multiple access computing machinery alongside shared faculty workspaces.

boxes.name: VIETNAM WAR CAMPUS POLITICS
boxes.description: Collect contemporary student newspaper archives, police records, and activist pamphlets documenting draft protests and antiwar sentiment around Cambridge in 1966.
boxes.rationale: The screenplay requires historical context for the moral friction between government-funded scientific research and rising antiwar resistance on campus.
boxes.summary: Cambridge saw rising antiwar activism and draft protests throughout 1966. Student groups organized newsletters and rallies demanding troop withdrawals from Vietnam. Institutional press releases and local publications documented campus unrest surrounding national military policies. Academic spaces operated in close proximity to street-level political resistance.

boxes.name: ACADEMIC HIERARCHY DRESS
boxes.description: Source faculty yearbooks, administrative portraits, and student snapshots illustrating the clothing distinctions among tenured professors, graduate assistants, and clerical staff.
boxes.rationale: Costume design must visually establish institutional rank and generational friction across the faculty and secretarial pool.
boxes.summary: MIT yearbooks and administrative portraits recorded distinct sartorial hierarchies in 1966. Tenured professors wore tailored suits, ties, and academic jackets. Graduate assistants and degree candidates dressed in less formal collared shirts and slacks. Clerical staff appeared in distinct professional daywear documented across institute photo archives.

boxes.name: EARLY HACKER LEXICON
boxes.description: Compile contemporary glossaries, faculty correspondence, and internal lab memos recording the technical jargon and casual slang used by MIT computer researchers in the mid-1960s.
boxes.rationale: Dialogue writers require period-accurate technical terminology to write naturalistic exchanges between computer scientists, secretaries, and students.
boxes.summary: MIT computing researchers developed a specialized internal dialect preserved in laboratory memos. Early jargon files document phrases originating in the Tech Model Railroad Club and Project MAC offices. Terms like crock, lose, and hacker described system failures and programming habits. This technical lexicon defined daily workplace dialogue between engineers.

boxes.name: MIDCENTURY MACHINE ACOUSTICS
boxes.description: Locate high-fidelity recordings and technical audio profiles of punch-card sorters, mainframe cooling blowers, magnetic tape drives, and Model 33 teletypewriters.
boxes.rationale: The sound department needs precise sonic references to build the dense industrial drone of mid-1960s data-processing facilities.
boxes.summary: The IBM 7094 machine room generated continuous mechanical noise from cooling blowers and magnetic tape drives. Teletypewriter terminals produced rhythmic percussive clatter during text input and printout. Period audio records document electronic tones and the sound of card-sorting machinery. Mainframe spaces relied on these dense industrial acoustic signatures.

boxes.name: CAMBRIDGE DAILY LIFE
boxes.description: Survey 1966 city street directories, cafeteria menus, public transit maps, and local retail records surrounding Massachusetts Avenue and Kendall Square.
boxes.rationale: The art and locations teams need verified period details to dress exterior scenes, institutional dining spaces, and faculty commute patterns.
boxes.summary: City directories and street maps established the commercial landscape of Kendall Square and Massachusetts Avenue. Local diners, retail shops, and transit routes served university staff during daily routines. Archival records map commuter movement through urban Cambridge blocks surrounding campus facilities. Cafeterias and small eateries formed the everyday infrastructure for institute workers.

boxes.name: COLD WAR DEFENSE FUNDING
boxes.description: Analyze 1966 federal grant records, institutional ledgers, and administrative correspondence linking MIT computer research programs to the Advanced Research Projects Agency.
boxes.rationale: The script department must accurately ground the political pressures and institutional funding dependencies that weighed upon Weizenbaum.
boxes.summary: The Advanced Research Projects Agency funded Project MAC through multi-year federal research contracts. Administrative files trace grant allocations from the Department of Defense to MIT computing directors. Ledgers linked university laboratories directly to Cold War defense planning. Institutional correspondence recorded regular fiscal reporting between campus administrators and military liaisons.

boxes.name: SECRETARIAL LABOR PRACTICES
boxes.description: Assemble oral histories, administrative manuals, and desk inventory photographs documenting the duties and workspace tools of MIT department secretaries in 1966.
boxes.rationale: The production needs precise staging references for Weizenbaum's secretary as she experiences ELIZA in private administrative sessions.
boxes.summary: Department secretaries maintained daily office operations using midcentury typewriters and paper files. Administrative inventories list standard desktop supplies, correspondence logs, and appointment records. Archival collections document secretarial responsibilities across faculty offices. Women performed essential clerical labor that supported computing projects and laboratory administration.

boxes.name: CAMBRIDGE ARCHITECTURAL FABRIC
boxes.description: Map existing midcentury brutalist buildings, vintage industrial brick structures, and preserved campus walkways across the 1966 MIT campus perimeter.
boxes.rationale: Location managers must secure shooting sites that match the visual density and material finishes of mid-1960s urban Cambridge.
boxes.summary: The MIT campus perimeter combined midcentury concrete brutalism with older industrial brick architecture. Numbered building complexes were linked by paved campus walkways and open access lots. Master plans preserved specific pedestrian routes between Cambridge streets and research complexes. Technology Square stood alongside this evolving midcentury urban fabric.

boxes.name: PSYCHIATRIC AND PSYCHOTHERAPY CULTURE
boxes.description: Gather 1960s Rogerian therapy transcripts, clinical psychology journals, and academic attitudes toward psychiatric dialogue that directly informed the design and unintended clinical reception of the ELIZA program.
boxes.rationale: This concept directly connects the central dramatic engine of Weizenbaum's software to secretarial confessional interactions, hacker perceptions, and academic ethical debates across the project.
boxes.summary: Carl Rogers popularized non-directive psychotherapy through recorded patient transcripts such as the Gloria sessions. Rogerian methodology relied on reflective statements and unconditional positive regard. ELIZA mirrored this clinical technique by turning typed statements into open-ended questions. Academic observers treated the program's conversational reflections as genuine psychiatric dialogue.

**Technology Square** was the nickname for MIT building NE43; its formal address was '545 Technology Square', but everyone just called it by the shortened form, **Tech Sq** .

The Technology Square complex contained other buildings; in about 1968 the Beta building, a virtual clone of the 545 Tech Square building, was built on the other side of the main courtyard, at 575 Tech Square. A Honeywell branch, [CISL](https://gunkies.org/w/index.php?title=CISL&action=edit&redlink=1 "CISL (page does not exist)") (probably 'Cambridge Information Systems Laboratory'), where much Multics work was done, was on the third floor of Beta. Computer Corporation of America was housed on the fifth floor of Beta.

Entrance sign

545 Tech Square held Project MAC \- later split into the AI Lab and the Laboratory for Computer Science (including the Dynamic Modeling, Mathlab, Macsyma Consortium, and Computer Systems Research - the group which did Multics, and a lot of early Internet work - groups), until they moved to the newly- and purpose-built [Stata Center](https://gunkies.org/w/index.php?title=Stata_Center&action=edit&redlink=1 "Stata Center (page does not exist)") in 2004. These entities housed, for many years, the vast majority of significant computer work at MIT

### Historical Note

The MIT Laboratory for Computer Science (LCS) was a laboratory for research in computer science and engineering, first established on July 1, 1963, as Project MAC in the Department of Electrical Engineering. By 1967 MAC had separated from the Electrical Engineering Department and started reporting directly to the MIT provost as an interdepartmental lab. The name Laboratory for Computer Science was chosen in 1975 and officially recognized in 1976. In 1981, while retaining its interdepartmental status, LCS came under the aegis of the School of Engineering, and the LCS director began reporting to the dean of engineering. On July 1, 2003, the Laboratory for Computer Science (LCS) merged with the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (AI) to form the MIT [Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory](http://www.csail.mit.edu/) (CSAIL).

When we are told to think of college activism that has had a long-lasting impact on the entire world, many of us might first think of the Vietnam War. # Project MAC

Timeline

One of the first major efforts supported by ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office (IPTO) was the Project on Mathematics and Computation (Project MAC), the world’s first large-scale experiment in personal computing, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

Orchestrated within the general context of broad-based command and control research suggested by the Office of the Secretary of Defense, and based on the vision of the founding IPTO Director, J.C.R. Licklider, Project MAC was oriented toward achieving a new level of human-computer interaction.

A major thrust of Project MAC was to develop general purpose time-sharing capabilities, which later influenced the design of computer systems for commercial and defense uses. Within years of its start, Project MAC would evolve into the world’s first online community, complete with online bulletin boards, email, virtual friendships, an open-source software exchange—and hackers.

## The IBM 7090

ALSO SEE:  
Columbia University Machine Room 1965 Photo Gallery  
Nine high-quality photos, four of them of the 7090.

The IBM 7090, announced in 1958, was a transistorized version of the
vacuum-tube-logic 709 and the first commercial computer with transistor
logic (the first such computing device, according to
 [53 ], was the IBM 608, but that was not a
general-purpose stored-program computer). The 7090, like the 700 series it
superseded, was intended mainly for scientific computing, but it was also
suitable for business and administrative use. Its IBSYS operating system
was tape-based; it required 8 magnetic tape drives run and had to be booted
from the card reader.

Columbia's 7090 was installed in 1963; by 1966 it had been upgraded to a
bigger and faster 7094 and coupled with a 7040 to form the 7094/7040 Directly
Coupled System, which would remain in place until 1968, when it was replaced
by the IBM 360/91 .

Teletype Model 33 - Wikipedia. The Teletype Corporation introduced the Model 33 as a commercial product in 1963, [ 7 ] after it had originally been designed for the United States Navy . [ 8 ] The Model 33 was produced in three versions: [ 5 ]
* Model 33 ASR (Automatic Send and Receive), which has a built-in eight-hole punched tape reader and tape punch;
[ edit ]
While the manufacturer called the Model 33 teleprinter with a tape punch and tape reader a "Model 33 ASR", many computer users used the shorter term "ASR-33".
[ edit ]
Teletype Model 33 ASR teleprinter keyboard with punched tape reader and punch. The left-front unit is the tape reader with its three-position START/STOP/FREE lever in the STOP position. A less-common tape reader had a four-position START/AUTO/STOP/FREE lever. In the AUTO position it could be commanded on and off remotely.
The interface between the paper tape reader and the rest of the terminal is completely mechanical, with power, clock, and eight data bits (which Teletype called "intelligence") all transmitted in parallel through metal levers.
Earlier Teletype machine designs, such as the Model 28 ASR, had allowed the user to operate the keyboard to punch tape while independently transmitting a previously punched tape, or to punch a tape while printing something else. Independent use of the paper tape punch and reader is not possible with the Model 33 ASR. [ 22 ] [ 23 ]

prior_art.premise: A period drama set at MIT in 1966, the year Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA.

neighbors.title: Her
neighbors.overview: In the not so distant future, Theodore, a lonely writer, purchases a newly developed operating system designed to meet the user's every need. To Theodore's surprise, a romantic relationship develops between him and his operating system. This unconventional love story blends science fiction and romance in a sweet tale that explores the nature of love and the ways that technology isolates and connects us all.

neighbors.title: Ex Machina
neighbors.overview: Caleb, a coder at the world's largest internet company, wins a competition to spend a week at a private mountain retreat belonging to Nathan, the reclusive CEO of the company. But when Caleb arrives at the remote location he finds that he will have to participate in a strange and fascinating experiment in which he must interact with the world's first true artificial intelligence, housed in the body of a beautiful robot girl.

neighbors.title: The Imitation Game
neighbors.overview: Second World War drama - A young woman decides against working in a munitions factory, and lands a post with the signals corps attempting to crack the Enigma code.

neighbors.title: To End All War: Oppenheimer & the Atomic Bomb
neighbors.overview: Explore how one man's relentless drive and invention of the atomic bomb changed the nature of war forever, led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people and unleashed mass hysteria.

neighbors.title: Oppenheimer
neighbors.overview: The story of J. Robert Oppenheimer's role in the development of the atomic bomb during World War II.

neighbors.title: Kinsey
neighbors.overview: Kinsey is a portrait of researcher Alfred Kinsey, driven to uncover the most private secrets of a nation. What begins for Kinsey as a scientific endeavor soon takes on an intensely personal relevance, ultimately becoming an unexpected journey into the mystery of human behavior.

The movie's plot is based on the true story of a group of young computer hackers from Hannover, Germany. In the late 1980s the orphaned Karl Koch invests his heritage in a flat and a home computer. At first he dials up to bulletin boards to discuss conspiracy theories inspired by his favorite novel, R.A. Wilson's "Illuminatus", but soon he and his friend David start breaking into government and military computers. Pepe, one of Karl's rather criminal acquaintances senses that there is money in computer cracking - he travels to east Berlin and tries to contact the KGB.

neighbors.title: A Beautiful Mind
neighbors.overview: From the heights of notoriety to the depths of depravity, John Forbes Nash Jr. experiences it all. As a brilliant but socially awkward mathematician, he made a groundbreaking discovery early in his career and stands on the brink of international acclaim. But as the handsome and arrogant Nash accepts secret work in cryptography, he becomes entangled in a mysterious conspiracy. His life takes a nightmarish turn and he soon finds himself on a painful and harrowing journey of self-discovery.

neighbors.title: Death Becomes Her
neighbors.overview: Madeline is married to Ernest, who was once her arch-rival Helen's fiancé. After recovering from a mental breakdown, Helen vows to kill Madeline and steal back Ernest. Unfortunately for everyone, the introduction of a magic potion causes things to be a great deal more complicated than a mere murder plot.

neighbors.title: Forrest Gump
neighbors.overview: A man with a low IQ has accomplished great things in his life and been present during significant historic events—in each case, far exceeding what anyone imagined he could do. But despite all he has achieved, his one true love eludes him.

neighbors.title: An Honest Liar
neighbors.overview: An Honest Liar tells the incredible story of the world-famous magician, escape artist, and world-renowned enemy of deception, James 'The Amazing' Randi. The film brings to life Randi's intricate investigations that publicly exposed psychics, faith healers, and con-artists with quasi-religious fervor. A master deceiver who came out of the closet at the age of 81, Randi created fictional characters, fake psychics, and even turned his partner of 25 years, Jose Alvarez, into a sham guru named Carlos.

neighbors.title: The Island
neighbors.overview: In 2019, Lincoln Six-Echo is a resident of a seemingly "Utopian" but contained facility. Like all of the inhabitants of this carefully-controlled environment, Lincoln hopes to be chosen to go to The Island — reportedly the last uncontaminated location on the planet. But Lincoln soon discovers that everything about his existence is a lie.
